short: The gap between what your drink recipes say the bar should have consumed and what it actually consumed in the same period.
seoTitle: Bar Variance: Theoretical vs Actual Liquor Cost
metaDescription: Bar variance is the gap between the liquor your recipes predict and what the bar actually used. What a normal gap looks like and what a wide one means.
definition: Bar variance is the difference between theoretical beverage cost — what the drinks you rang up should have consumed, according to your recipes and pour sizes — and actual beverage cost, calculated from opening stock plus purchases minus closing stock. A small gap is normal in any venue. A wide one is money leaving the building, and the value of the measure is that it narrows a vague suspicion to a number you can act on.

formula.expression: Actual cost = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock; Variance = Actual cost % − Theoretical cost %
formula.note: Both percentages are taken against beverage sales for the same period. Around a point of variance is ordinary; three or more points warrants investigation.

bodyHtml:
What a wide gap usually means

The list is short and worth working through in order, cheapest first. Free-pouring that runs generous. Drinks served and never rung up. Breakage and spillage nobody recorded. Comps and staff drinks outside the system. A house pour that has quietly become a premium brand. And last, stock leaving the premises. Measurement problems are far more common than theft, and they are much cheaper to fix.

Count weekly, not monthly

A monthly count tells you something went wrong in the last thirty days, which is rarely enough to act on. A weekly count tells you which week, and often which shift. For spirits at least, weekly is the interval at which the number becomes useful rather than merely interesting.

Rule out arithmetic first

Before treating a gap as leakage, check that the pours-per-bottle figure in your pricing matches the one in your stock valuation, and that every recipe reflects what is actually served. A bar that prices on twenty-five pours and pours twenty-three will show a permanent variance that no amount of supervision will close, because nothing is going missing.

faq.question: What is an acceptable bar variance?
faq.answer: Around one point between theoretical and actual cost is ordinary in a working bar and not worth chasing. Three or four points is worth investigating, and anything consistently wider than that usually has a specific and findable cause. What matters more than the absolute figure is the trend: a variance that is stable is a known cost, and one that is widening is a live problem.

faq.question: Do I need a POS to measure bar variance?
faq.answer: You need a reliable record of what was sold and a reliable count of what is on the shelf. A point-of-sale system makes the sales side easy, but a bar with a disciplined manual count and an accurate sales summary can calculate the same figure. The stock count is the harder half — without a trustworthy closing stock there is no actual cost to compare against.
